title: Phalut to Rimbik: The Long Way Down
meta_description: The Singalila trek beyond Sandakphu: the 21 km ridge to Phalut, down to Gorkhey, Samanden and Rammam, and out via Srikhola to Rimbik, with stages and costs.
summary: Beyond Sandakphu, the Singalila trail runs 21 km along the ridge to Phalut, where West Bengal, Sikkim and Nepal meet, then drops about 1,200 m to Gorkhey and winds through the roadless villages of Samanden and Rammam to Srikhola and Rimbik. Allow three to four days from Sandakphu. It is the quietest and greenest part of the trek.

sections.heading: Why go beyond Sandakphu
paras: Most people who reach Sandakphu turn round, ride a Land Rover down or drop straight to Srikhola. Those who carry on north find a different trek. The ridge to Phalut is open grassland and dwarf rhododendron facing Kanchenjunga nearly all day. Phalut itself is a lonely summit on a tri-junction of borders. And the descent passes through farming villages with no road, where families still carry everything up from Rimbik and the evenings are quiet except for cattle bells and the river.

This section adds three or four days to the classic trek, for six to seven days in all from Maneybhanjan. It suits walkers who are already acclimatised and enjoying the trail, and who want fewer people and more forest. Your licensed guide comes with you the whole way; the guide mandate applies throughout Singalila National Park, so check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Sandakphu to Phalut
paras: This is the longest day of the whole Singalila trek and, on a clear day, the finest. The trail leaves Sandakphu northward along the crest, passing the hump of Sabargram at about 3,536 m, and runs over open, rolling ground with Kanchenjunga ahead and Everest and Makalu over your left shoulder. There are no lodges or shops between the two summits, only an SSB post or two and the occasional herders' shelter, so carry a packed lunch, at least 2 litres of water each and a warm layer.

Start by 7 am. Cloud often rises from the valleys by early afternoon, and the ridge is exposed to wind. If the weather turns bad before Sabargram, the sensible choice is to go back to Sandakphu and try again the next day. A jeep track runs along much of this stretch, used by park and SSB vehicles and sometimes by Land Rovers for Phalut trips; walking it is easy but long. Land Rover runs to Phalut and the condition of the track change with the season, so check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: A night at Phalut
paras: Phalut, at about 3,600 m, is the second-highest point in West Bengal and the place where West Bengal, Sikkim and Nepal meet. North of it the Singalila Ridge runs on into West Sikkim toward the high country below Kanchenjunga, which from here is only about 55 km away and fills the whole northern sky. On most autumn days you share the summit with a handful of trekkers, the border guards and the wind.

Accommodation is very limited: a government trekkers' hut that has not always been open, and in some seasons nothing else. Some groups walk from Sandakphu to Phalut for sunset and continue down to Gorkhey the same day, a very long day of 9–10 hours; others carry on early next morning after sunrise. Ask your guide in Maneybhanjan which option is possible on your dates, and check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Down to Gorkhey
paras: Below Phalut the trail finally leaves the crest and drops, losing about 1,200 m over roughly 15 km. You pass through every band of the ridge forest in reverse: dwarf rhododendron and juniper, then silver fir hung with lichen, then tall rhododendron, oak and thick bamboo. In April and May this descent is among the best rhododendron walks on the trek, and it is good red panda and bird country throughout. The path is steep, rocky and often wet, so trekking poles and good boots matter.

Gorkhey sits where the forest opens beside the Gorkhey Khola, a cold stream in the Rammam river system. After days on the bare ridge it feels green and sheltered, with a handful of farmhouses, potato and maize fields, cattle on the meadow and a few family lodges. There is no road; supplies come in on foot or by mule. Many trekkers say this first night off the ridge is their favourite of the whole trip.

sections.heading: Samanden and Rammam
paras: From Gorkhey a stiff climb takes you out of the valley to Samanden, a small hamlet in a bowl of terraced fields at roughly 2,500 m, where a few families take trekkers as homestay guests. It is a short stage, and many groups walk straight on, but a night here is the closest this trek comes to the old pattern of Himalayan travel: you sleep where there is space and eat what the family eats.

Beyond Samanden the trail runs along the slope to Rammam, a larger village at about 2,560 m with a school, family lodges and fields above the valley. The village shares its name with the Rammam river, which rises in the Singalila range and flows east, forming part of the boundary between Darjeeling district and Sikkim before joining the Rangeet near Jorethang. From Rammam it is a long, steady descent through forest and farmland to Srikhola.

If you have a spare day, spend it at Gorkhey. Walk up the stream for an hour, sit by the water, watch the farm work and let your legs recover from the descent. It is one of the few places on the trek where there is nothing to climb and nowhere to be.

sections.heading: Srikhola, Rimbik and getting home
paras: Srikhola, at about 1,900 m, is the warm bottom of the trek: a bridge over the Sri Khola, riverside lodges and the sound of water. The jeep road now reaches here, and jeeps run to Rimbik in 30–45 minutes for about ₹50–100 a seat, or ₹600–1,000 reserved. Many trekkers spend their last night by the river and take an early jeep the next morning.

Rimbik, at about 2,286 m, is the small market centre for these villages, with lodges, shops and a Tuesday market. Shared jeeps for Darjeeling leave early, mostly between 6 and 7.30 am, and take 4–5 hours for about ₹200–300 a seat; a reserved jeep costs ₹3,000–4,500. Departure times change with the season, so confirm the evening before and check current status before you travel. Tip your guide and porter here, at the end of the walk.

sections.heading: Costs and practical notes
paras: Lodges on the descent are simpler and often a little cheaper than at Sandakphu, with beds or twin rooms at about ₹500–1,200 per person and dinner and breakfast at ₹400–700, frequently quoted as a package. Hot water comes by the bucket for ₹50–100. Carry enough cash for the whole descent; there is no ATM before Rimbik, and signal is weak or absent in the valley villages.
list: Count on three nights from Sandakphu to Srikhola, or four with a night at Samanden.
Start the Phalut day early, carry lunch and water, and turn back in bad weather.
Use trekking poles for the 1,200 m drop to Gorkhey; knees take more strain than lungs here.
Expect leeches in the lower forest after rain in late spring and early autumn.
Bring a little extra cash for porters, since many trekkers hire one for the long Phalut day.

faqs.q: How far is Phalut from Sandakphu?
faqs.a: About 21 km along the Singalila Ridge, via Sabargram at about 3,536 m. It takes most walkers 7–8 hours. There are no lodges or shops on the way, so carry a packed lunch, at least 2 litres of water and warm layers, start by 7 am and turn back if cloud and wind come in early.

Only very limited. There is a government trekkers' hut that has not always been open, and in some seasons no other lodging. Some groups go from Sandakphu to Phalut and continue down to Gorkhey the same day. Ask your guide at Maneybhanjan which plan is possible on your dates, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How difficult is the descent from Phalut to Gorkhey?
faqs.a: Moderately hard on the legs. The trail drops about 1,200 m over roughly 15 km through forest, steep and rocky in places and often wet. Lungs have an easy day but knees do not. Trekking poles and boots with good grip help a lot. Most walkers take 5–6 hours, with breaks.

faqs.q: Is there a road to Gorkhey or Samanden?
faqs.a: No. Gorkhey, Samanden and Rammam have no motor road, and supplies come in on foot or by mule. The nearest jeep point is Srikhola, roughly half a day's walk from Rammam. That is part of what makes these villages quiet, and why lodges are simple and food depends on what the family has.

faqs.q: How many days does the Phalut route add to the Sandakphu trek?
faqs.a: About two days compared with the short descent from Sandakphu to Srikhola. The full trek from Maneybhanjan via Sandakphu, Phalut, Gorkhey and Rammam to Srikhola usually takes six to seven days, plus a night in Darjeeling at each end. Add a day if you want to sleep at Samanden or rest at Gorkhey.

faqs.q: Can I go to Phalut by Land Rover?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Land Rovers from Maneybhanjan have run trips to Phalut along the ridge track, at a higher rate than the Sandakphu round trip. Whether they run depends on the track, the season and park rules, and accommodation at Phalut is limited. Ask at the Maneybhanjan association counter and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Where does the Sandakphu Phalut trek end?
faqs.a: At Srikhola, where the jeep road now reaches, or Rimbik, 30–45 minutes further by jeep. From Rimbik, shared jeeps leave early for Darjeeling, mostly between 6 and 7.30 am, taking 4–5 hours for about ₹200–300 a seat. Confirm times the evening before, as they change with the season.

faqs.q: Is the Phalut descent good for rhododendrons?
faqs.a: Yes. The forest below Phalut, from fir and dwarf rhododendron near the top to tall rhododendron, oak and bamboo lower down, is one of the best rhododendron walks on the trek in April and May. The upper ridge to Phalut flowers later, in May, and timing shifts by a couple of weeks each year.

faqs.q: Are there homestays at Samanden and Rammam?
faqs.a: Yes, simple ones. A few families at Samanden take trekkers as homestay guests, and Rammam has family lodges. Expect about ₹500–1,200 per person for a bed and ₹400–700 for dinner and breakfast, often as a package. Rooms are basic, food is home cooking and your guide usually arranges the night.
